title: Try a new case
subtitle: An optional written transfer check after the ten chapters
intro: Try this fictional case without your notes. Allow twenty to thirty minutes. Write somewhere private; this page does not collect or grade your answers. Compare with the suggested reasoning after your attempt.
paragraphs: A library’s book-return shelf moves behind a locked door. Missed returns rise. A coordinator calls users lazy and compares raw counts across branches with different numbers of loans.

A chime reliably precedes opening time. Visitors begin preparing to enter on hearing it. Separately, a reminder tone stops after a return and returns increase. The coordinator calls both examples punishment.

A learner watches a shelving demonstration and can explain the rule but has not tried a new case. A cue response decreases in one room and returns elsewhere. An app promises every routine becomes a habit in a fixed number of days.
The library wants a consensual procedure that improves access and reliable returns without surveillance or coercion.

tasks.title: Define and measure
tasks.prompt: Identify an operational outcome, denominator and likely access barrier.
tasks.answer: Define a return to an accessible marked location within a stated period, record opportunities per loan and compare comparable windows. The locked door may block performance even when the skill exists.

tasks.title: Identify learning relations
tasks.prompt: Distinguish the chime from tone removal and explain what schedule information is missing.
tasks.answer: The chime is a possible predictive conditioned cue. Tone removal is negative reinforcement if it follows returns and increases them. A schedule requires the actual response-count or timing rule, not just the name of a reward.

tasks.title: Context and transfer
tasks.prompt: Interpret response return and plan a fair generalization check.
tasks.answer: A context-related return is consistent with renewal; extinction need not erase prior learning. Use safe varied examples and boundary cases, checking delayed responding across relevant settings.

tasks.title: Observation and habit
tasks.prompt: How would you test learning from the demonstration and the habit promise?
tasks.answer: Use an independent new shelving case after a delay. Explanation and imitation differ. Habit concerns cue-linked tendencies, and its development varies; no fixed day count establishes every routine.

tasks.title: A useful and ethical intervention
tasks.prompt: Design a proportionate evaluation with participant agency.
tasks.answer: Agree a meaningful goal, restore access, teach any missing skill and record repeated comparable outcomes with consent. Consider alternative changes, harms and acceptability. Check maintenance and transfer without withdrawing essential support.

rubric.title: Accurate distinctions
rubric.strong: Explains the relevant concepts and separates observations from interpretations.
rubric.developing: Adds labels without explaining how the evidence supports them.

rubric.title: Evidence and alternatives
rubric.strong: Considers competing explanations and a comparison that could distinguish them.
rubric.developing: Treats a plausible account, score or correlation as a settled cause.

rubric.title: Proportionate application
rubric.strong: States limitations, respects the people involved and explains what would change the recommendation.
rubric.developing: Overgeneralizes to individuals or makes a recommendation beyond the evidence.

followup: Return tomorrow or in a week with an unfamiliar example. Compare the quality of your explanation, not just your confidence. This self-check does not certify professional competence or establish general mastery.
